title: Australians back super support for unpaid carers
full_text:
Almost two-thirds of Australians with superannuation support government-funded super top-ups for eligible people taking time out of paid work to care for family, according to research commissioned by Australian Retirement Trust (ART).
The YouGov survey found 65 per cent supported the measure, while 16 per cent opposed it. Support was higher among women, at 71 per cent, compared with 58 per cent of men.
The findings also showed 67 per cent believed support should include super contributions while people were caring, rather than relying only on Age Pension support in retirement.
With National Carers Week taking place from 11-18 October, the research found 81 per cent identified time out of paid work to care for children or other family members as one of the top three reasons women retire with less super than men.
That placed caring responsibilities ahead of lower average earnings, identified by 52 per cent, and part-time or casual work, nominated by 48 per cent.
ART acting chief people and impact officer Anne Fuchs said closing the gender super gap should involve support beyond individuals and their families.
“What this shows is that Australians recognise the impact unpaid care can have on retirement savings,” Fuchs said. “There’s a lot an individual can do, but closing the gender super gap should not be left to women and their families alone.”
The fund cited Super Members Council research showing women were three times more likely than men to take on unpaid caring, and accounted for more than 70 per cent of people who stepped out of paid work to provide intensive care.
Separate council research cited by ART put the difference between women’s and men’s super balances at retirement age at around $50,000.
Fuchs said the survey findings showed Australians understood how unpaid caring responsibilities contributed to the retirement savings gap.
“Super is helping Australians retire confidently. But time out to care for someone isn’t paid, and it doesn’t build super,” Fuchs said. “In many cases this care is done by women, and it’s a big part of why they retire with less.”
The online survey of 1,011 adults was conducted between 17 and 23 September, with results weighted to represent Australian adults aged 18 and over with superannuation. Its questions covered time out of paid work for parenting, as well as caring for an older or unwell relative.
